report:
## Conclusion
The claim is **not false** — it's well supported by good-quality evidence, though not unanimous. The largest and most rigorous randomized trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine (Tuuli et al., 2016), found that chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep before cesarean delivery significantly lowered surgical-site infection rates compared with iodine-alcohol (~4% vs ~7-9%), for both superficial and deep infections (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048).

However, the evidence is mixed, not unanimous. Subsequent trials have not all replicated this benefit. The CAPICA trial found **no significant difference** between chlorhexidine-alcohol and povidone-iodine (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/), and a smaller pilot RCT similarly found comparable infection rates (~4.5% vs 4.6%) between groups (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/). A more recent systematic review and network meta-analysis of RCTs concluded that alcohol-based chlorhexidine had the *highest probability* of being most effective, but credible intervals for all compared antiseptics overlapped, meaning the difference did not reach clear statistical certainty across the combined evidence base (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282).

**Bottom line:** The single largest RCT to date favors chlorhexidine-alcohol, and it remains the intervention with the best point-estimate performance in meta-analyses. But because later trials (including CAPICA) failed to confirm superiority, and pooled network meta-analyses show overlapping confidence, the claim should be characterized as "supported by the best single trial but not definitively proven across all evidence" rather than outright false. Guidelines (e.g., CDC, WHO) generally recommend chlorhexidine-alcohol as a preferred option, but acknowledge some uncertainty remains.
